analysis.title: Global Metals Weekly: The battle for critical minerals
key_insights: China's copper demand fell 8% YoY in September, driven by a pullback in grid spending. FAI in electricity and heat generation fell 7% YoY in August. Decline rates in both have started to bottom out.
The physical copper market is tight despite weak Chinese demand. China's domestic inventories have declined gradually, Shanghai premia are at an all-time high, and consumers struggle to source units.
Profitable US warehouse-financing deals have pulled spare copper into North America, leaving the world ex-US undersupplied. Tight mine supply contributed less than the financing deals.
LME copper forward curves have moved into deeper backwardation. One trader holds 50-79% of cash positions, so the market is easy to squeeze.

BofA keeps seeing copper upside into next year despite soft Chinese consumption, because constrained availability should support prices. It forecasts $13,331/t for 2026 and $15,500/t for 2027, with deficits in both years.

Data centres and AI add to metals demand. Hyperscale sites are far more metals intensive than enterprise sites: 1.8-2.2x for cloud hyperscalers and 2.5-3.0x for AI hyperscalers, against 1x for enterprise.
Hyperscale data centres use 23,900 t/GW of copper and 6,200 t/GW of aluminium, against 10,600 and 2,600 for enterprise sites. They use 708,000 oz/GW of silver against 318,000 for enterprise.
BofA's forecast has data centre capacity rising from 114 GW in 2025 to 241 GW in 2030, with data centre electricity use rising from 1.72% to 3.05% of total.
Electrification sectors (grid, data centres/AI, EVs) hold roughly 40% of copper demand. BofA expects them to deliver as much demand growth in 2026-30 as the whole market did in the past decade.

Caveats to data centre metals demand: fast efficiency gains in AI energy use, power constraints, permitting, social acceptability, and a high-bandwidth memory shortage expected to last through at least the end of 2027.

The US and EU no longer treat critical minerals as a purely commercial issue. Tools include public finance, domestic mining and processing incentives, diversified sourcing, bilateral deals, price floors, contracts for difference and stockpiles.
The suitable policy tool depends on market size. Price floors that are affordable in rare earths may be too costly in copper, aluminium or steel, where trade measures dominate.
The EU has selected 93 strategic projects plus 13 outside the EU, and public actors have mobilised more than EUR 2bn.

Korea Zinc plans a $7.4bn US smelter with the US government, targeting trial operations in 2029. More than 90% of the cost is funded by the US government and strategic investors, including a $4.7bn DoW loan and a $0.21bn CHIPS Act grant.

The US launched Project Vault in 2026, a $12bn public-private stockpiling initiative. Glencore and Mercuria each committed $500mn. The US$20bn of notional US copper inventories is privately funded and not part of Project Vault.

A ruling on a US refined copper tariff is expected before January 2027. If no tariff comes, the CME curve would likely flatten and some warehoused copper could return to the market. BofA thinks a flood is unlikely and expects time-spread volatility to self-correct.
Producer countries use export restrictions to force downstream processing. UNCTAD counts nearly 100 new critical-mineral export measures since 2020: DRC 18, China 16, Indonesia 12.
Brazil's President Lula signed Law No. 15,506/2026 on 16 September 2026, creating the National Policy on Critical and Strategic Minerals.

The IEA estimates about $60bn of investment over a decade could diversify magnet rare-earth supply, against about $6.5tn of annual downstream sales exposed to disruption. Tripling rare-earth prices would add about 0.1% to a car's cost.
BofA is bullish on aluminium, copper, gold, silver and platinum/palladium, and neutral on lead, nickel and zinc. It sees aluminium deficits in 2026 and 2027 and a copper deficit of 272kt in 2027.
BofA forecasts gold at $5,093/oz for 2026 and $4,925/oz for 2027, and silver at $86/oz for 2026 and $74/oz for 2027. Silver is expected to be in surplus in 2026 (910 tonnes).

sector_views.rationale: Constrained ex-US availability, LME backwardation and electrification demand support prices, with deficits expected in 2026 and 2027.
Consumers in Europe and the US are competing for units, supply additions have slowed, and BofA expects deficits in 2026 and 2027.
Gold is a hedge against US policy uncertainty, and BofA sees upside risk to its forecasts.
Production discipline and new applications such as solar rebalanced the market, though the outlook beyond 2026 is less clear because of substitution risk.
Platinum stays in deficit and should outperform palladium, which could be tight on production issues.
Indonesia is slowing output growth, with a deficit expected in 2026 and a surplus in 2027.
Mine supply is tight and LME inventories are low, but BofA expects a surplus in 2026 and 2027.
No immediate scrap or concentrate shortages, so the market could flip back into surplus.
Production keeps rising, which should create a surplus next year, and China's steel mills face overcapacity pressure.

macro_indicators.interpretation: Weak Chinese consumption, driven by lower grid spending, with the rate of decline starting to bottom out.

macro_indicators.indicator: China FAI in electricity and heat generation
macro_indicators.interpretation: Grid investment slowdown weighs on copper demand and makes China's 5-year plan electrification target harder to reach.
BofA says this would be the weakest since 1988.
BofA sees upside into next year because supply is constrained.
The market moves from a small surplus in 2026 to a deficit in 2027.
Appendix market snapshot spot level, +1.5% YoY.

risk_factors: A decision not to impose a US refined copper tariff could flatten the CME curve and release warehoused copper.
Trade wars hurting sentiment, listed as a downside risk for every base metal.
China re-exporting copper, or global demand slowing sharply into next year.
Rapid AI efficiency gains, power constraints, permitting limits and social pushback could slow data centre metals demand.
A high-bandwidth memory shortage expected to last through at least the end of 2027.
Silver substitution in solar could accelerate, and ETF liquidation could hit gold and silver.
Real rates turning more positive or a sustained USD rally for gold.
China not exporting refined zinc keeps the LME squeeze going, while unreported zinc inventories could ease it.

vol_and_positioning: LME copper cash-to-3-month spreads have moved into deeper backwardation.
One trader holds 50-79% of LME cash warrant positions, which raises squeeze risk.
LME zinc inventories are very low and have led to periodic short squeezes.
Cancelled warrants as a share of LME stocks: copper 17.6%, zinc 17.8%, lead 22.2%, aluminium 5.9%, nickel 6.7%, tin 10.2%.
The CME copper curve is in steep contango, which makes warehouse-financing deals profitable.

tension_points.bull_case: Warehouse financing pulls metal to the US, LME backwardation deepens and one trader holds 50-79% of cash positions, so BofA sees upside into next year and a 2027 deficit of 272kt.
tension_points.bear_case: A no-tariff decision would flatten the CME curve and could release warehoused copper, and weak Chinese demand (-8% YoY in September) persists.
tension_points.what_invalidates: A US ruling against a refined copper tariff, expected before January 2027, that flattens the CME curve and lets warehoused copper return to the market.

tension_points.bull_case: Hyperscale sites are 1.8-3.0x as metals intensive as enterprise sites, and electrification sectors should match the whole market's past-decade copper demand growth in 2026-30.
tension_points.bear_case: AI energy efficiency is improving fast, and power, permitting and community pushback constrain build-out.
